summary: Describes why quality of service and media authorization are needed in SIP and defines a private extension that ties QoS admission control to call signaling. It helps guard against denial of service attacks. It applies only within administrative domains, or federations of them, that have agreed on policies in advance.

eli5.summary: A theme park checks your ticket before letting you onto a fast ride. This extension lets a phone network check a call is approved before giving it reserved bandwidth.

questions: how does sip integrate qos admission control
how does qos work with sip
subtitle: Tying quality-of-service admission control to SIP call signaling

tldr.problem: Networks need to control access to reserved bandwidth during calls to prevent denial of service attacks and manage resources fairly. However, call signaling and resource reservation are typically separate processes.
tldr.mechanism: A SIP proxy provides authorization tokens in a P-Media-Authorization header field during call setup, which the calling and called terminals then include in resource reservation requests to prove they are authorized for QoS.
tldr.outcome: This extension helps manage network resources and defend against fraud, but it only works within closed administrative domains because it requires end-to-end message body inspection and hop-by-hop security.

today: RFC 3313 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains the specification for this SIP extension, which is used in cable telephony and 3G mobile networks that implement the PacketCable and 3GPP standards.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
This RFC defines a private extension to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) that ties quality of service (QoS) admission control to call signaling. In modern IP networks, bandwidth is a shared resource, and uncontrolled access to reserved bandwidth can lead to denial of service attacks and unfair resource allocation. This extension allows a SIP proxy to authorize QoS requests before a call's media streams can consume network resources.

The mechanism is designed specifically for closed environments like cable networks or mobile networks where a single administrative domain controls both the SIP proxies and the network QoS policies. It does not apply to the open Internet, where message bodies might be encrypted and multiple trust boundaries exist.
sections.eli5: Phone networks need to check that calls are allowed before they reserve expensive network bandwidth. This extension links the permission checking with the call setup, using permission tokens.

sections.title: Architecture and Components
sections.content:
The extension assumes a simplified architecture with four main participants: a user agent client (UAC) that initiates calls, a user agent server (UAS) that receives them, an originating proxy (OP) that handles the caller's side, and a destination proxy (DP) that handles the called party's side. Each proxy interfaces with a policy decision point (PDP) that generates authorization tokens based on admission control policies.

When a call is initiated, the originating proxy receives the SIP INVITE message, authenticates the caller, and consults its PDP to obtain an authorization token. This token is returned to the caller in a P-Media-Authorization header within provisional or final response messages. The caller then includes this token when requesting network resources via a separate reservation protocol such as RSVP.
sections.eli5: There are four players: the caller, the called party, two special phone company computers that handle each side, and permission servers that generate approval tokens. The tokens flow from the permission servers through the phone company computers to the callers.

sections.title: The P-Media-Authorization Header
sections.content:
The P-Media-Authorization header field is a private extension that carries one or more media authorization tokens as hexadecimal strings. Each token is formatted as a Policy-Element as defined in RFC 2750, and represents permission for the associated media stream to receive QoS treatment. The header can appear in SIP INVITE messages, provisional responses (except 100), and final 2xx responses.

Each token encodes information about what QoS is authorized, and is typically generated by the network's policy decision point. The tokens are opaque to the end terminals, which simply extract them from SIP messages and pass them to the resource reservation mechanism. The header is restricted to messages that carry offer or answer information (SDP), since QoS authorization is meaningful only when media streams are being described.
sections.eli5: The header is like a stamped permission slip in the phone company's secret code. It contains approval for a specific amount of reserved network bandwidth, and both the caller and called party carry it to the network's admission control system.

sections.title: Call Flow and Resource Reservation
sections.content:
A call begins when the user agent client sends an INVITE to the originating proxy. The proxy authenticates the caller, checks with its policy decision point whether the caller is authorized for QoS, and obtains authorization tokens. These tokens are included in responses sent back to the UAC. Upon receiving the response containing the P-Media-Authorization header, the UAC stores the tokens and converts them to Policy-Elements, which it then includes in RSVP PATH messages to request bandwidth from the network.

The edge router or admission control system at the network edge receives the RSVP message, checks the Policy-Element against the authorization policy stored in its PDP, and either grants or denies the reservation. Once both directions of the media stream have been authorized and admitted, media can flow. The same pattern applies at the called party's side, with the destination proxy providing authorization tokens for the called terminal.
sections.eli5: The call setup happens in steps: the caller asks permission, the phone company checks and sends back an approval token, the caller presents the token to the network, the network checks it and reserves bandwidth. The same thing happens on the called party's side.

sections.title: Security and Applicability Constraints
sections.content:
This extension requires that media authorization tokens be protected from eavesdropping and tampering during transit from proxy to terminal. However, SIP provides only hop-by-hop protection mechanisms such as TLS or IPSec; if intermediaries are present, they can access the authorization tokens in cleartext, enabling theft of service and denial of service attacks. There is currently no standard way to provide end-to-end encryption of SIP headers, so the extension mandates that proxies must not send tokens through untrusted intermediaries.

Additionally, the extension requires that message bodies describing media (such as SDP) not be encrypted end-to-end, so that proxies can inspect them to decide what QoS to authorize. This breaks end-to-end confidentiality of media descriptions. Because of these limitations, the mechanism is suitable only for closed administrative domains such as cable networks, 3G mobile networks, or other environments where all nodes are under trusted control.
sections.eli5: The permission tokens must be protected from prying eyes, but the system can only protect them between neighbors in the phone network, not all the way to the caller. Also, the phone company must be able to read the media descriptions to decide what permission to give. So this only works in trusted phone company networks, not on the open Internet.
